message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "cli-and-output" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: Only argv[1] is used; all arguments from argv[2] onward are silently ignored (no error, no extra output, nothing on stderr).
  Their claimed evidence: $ cd /workspace/dataset
$ ./test4_executable "a" "b" "例子.测试" | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n     # == result for "a" alone
$ ./test4_executable "a" | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n

$ ./test4_executable "例子.测试" "a" "b" | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n   1  \n     # == result for "例子.测试" alone
$ ./test4_executable "例子.测试" | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n   1  \n

$ ./test4_executable "" "example.com" | od -c
0000000   0  \n   0  \n   1  \n   0  \n     # empty argv[1] wins; argv[2] ignored

$ ./test4_executable "例子.测试" 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 | od -c        # 8 args
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n   1  \n
$ ./test4_executable "例子.测试" $(seq 1 49) | od -c            # 50 args
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n   1  \n

$ ./test4_executable a b c 2>/tmp/e4 >/dev/null; wc -c /tmp/e4
0 /tmp/e4

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

cd /workspace/dataset
rep(){ local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
# diverse argv[1] values incl. invalid UTF-8, high bytes, single chars, boundary lengths
V=( "" "a" "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" \
    "example.com" "例子.测试" "xn--fsqu00a.xn--0zwm56d" "ä" "ÿ" "€" "𐍈" \
    "$(printf '\xff')" "$(printf '\x80')" "$(printf '\xc3')" "$(printf '\xe4\xbd')" "$(printf '\xed\xa0\x80')" \
    "$(printf '\xf4\x90\x80\x80')" "$(printf '\x00')" "$(printf '\t')" "$(printf '\n')" "$(printf ' ')" \
    "$(rep 63 a)" "$(rep 64 a)" "$(rep 255 a)" "$(rep 256 a)" "$(rep 1000 a)" \
    "A.CoM" "1.2.3.4" "-" "_" "$(printf 'a\xffb.com')" )
# extra-arg patterns
declare -a P=( 'b' '' 'example.com' '例子.测试' '-' '--' '--help' '-h' 'a b' './test4_executable' )
fail=0
for v in "${V[@]}"; do
  base=$(./test4_executable "$v" 2>/tmp/eb | tr '\n' ','); ebb=$(wc -c </tmp/eb)
  for p in "${P[@]}"; do
    g=$(./test4_executable "$v" "$p" 2>/tmp/eg | tr '\n' ','); ebg=$(wc -c </tmp/eg)
    if [ "$base" != "$g" ] || [ "$ebb" != "$ebg" ]; then
      echo "DIFF argv1=$(printf '%q' "$v") extra=$(printf '%q' "$p") base=$base got=$g errB=$ebb errG=$ebg"; fail=1
    fi

  # also 3 extras and 20 extras
  g3=$(./test4_executable "$v" x y z 2>&1 | tr '\n' ',')

done

I attacked this from every angle I could and failed to break it. Summary of what I ran against `/workspace/dataset/test4_executable`:

**Re-ran their evidence** — all confirmed byte-for-byte (`rc=0`, stderr empty in every case).

**Attacks that found nothing:**

1. **argc sweep** — argv[1]=`例子.测试` plus 0..4096 extra args (argc 1→4097). Output `1\n1\n0\n1\n` at every count, stderr always 0 bytes.
2. **Differential matrix** — 40 argv[1] values (empty, single chars, `.`/`..`/`a..b`, invalid UTF-8 `\xff`/`\x80`/`\xc3`/lone surrogate `\xed\xa0\x80`/out-of-range `\xf4\x90\x80\x80`, tab/newline/space, lengths 63/64/255/256/1000) × 12 extra-arg patterns + 3-extras + 20-extras = 480 combos. Zero divergences.
3. **Randomized fuzz via direct `execve`** (Rust harness at `/tmp/fz/f.rs`, no shell, raw non-UTF-8 bytes in args) — 4000 argv[1] values × random 0-5 extras, 8000 process spawns. `diffs=0`, and the shape invariant held universally: stdout exactly 8 bytes, stderr empty, rc 0.
4. **getopt hypothesis** (the most promising lead) — if the program parsed flags it would skip argv[1] and consume argv[2]. `./test4_executable --help "例子.测试"` → `1\n1\n1\n0\n`, i.e. the result for the literal string `--help`, **not** the IDN result `1\n1\n0\n1\n`. Same for `--`, `-`, `-h`, `-v`, `--version`, `-x`, `-i`, `--input`, `--domain`. No flag parsing exists.
5. **"Only argv[1]" tested literally** — `exec -a WEIRD-NAME` and `exec -a ""` change nothing, so argv[0] is unused too. Locale/env (`LC_ALL=C`, `C.UTF-8`, `en_US.UTF-8`, `tr_TR.UTF-8`, `zh_CN.gb18030`, `env -i`), stdin (data / `/dev/null`), and cwd all have zero effect.
6. **Byte-exact `cmp`** of both stdout and stderr with vs. without 6 extra args across 12 inputs — identical files. 50-run determinism check: single unique output.

**One imprecision worth flagging (not a refutation).** The unqualified "no error, nothing on stderr" fails at the kernel's `execve` limit, before the binary runs. Bisected exactly:

```
$ s=$(head -c 131071 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'b'); ./test4_executable "例子.测试" "$s"   # rc=0, 8B stdout
$ s=$(head -c 131072 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'b'); ./test4_executable "例子.测试" "$s"
/bin/bash: ./test4_executable: Argument list too long        # rc=126, 0 bytes stdout
```

That is `MAX_ARG_STRLEN` (131072), a per-argument limit — confirmed by the control: two args of 131071 bytes each (262142 B total) succeed fine, so it is not total size. The total-list limit (`ARG_MAX` = 2097152) trips separately between 2000 and 2100 extras of 1000 B. In both cases the process never starts, so this is environmental rather than a property of the binary's argument handling. I did not treat it as a counterexample.

Verdict: **the rule holds**. I logged a sharpened wording in `correctedStatement`.

input.rule: Only argv[1] is used; all arguments from argv[2] onward are silently ignored (no error, no extra output, nothing on stderr).
input.correctedStatement: Directionally correct and verified across ~9,000 invocations; only sharpened for precision. Precise version: The program's entire output is a pure function of the single byte string argv[1]. If argc >= 2 it evaluates argv[1] verbatim (including empty string, raw non-UTF-8 bytes, and flag-looking values such as "-", "--", "--help", which are treated as ordinary domain strings, NOT parsed as options); if argc == 1 it evaluates the literal default "example.com". Everything else is ignored: argv[2..argc-1] (verified for argc 1..4097), argv[0] (verified via `exec -a WEIRD-NAME` and `exec -a ""`), the environment and locale (LC_ALL/LANG variants and `env -i` all identical), stdin, and cwd. In every run where the process actually starts, stdout is exactly 8 bytes (four "1"/"0" lines each terminated by \n), stderr is exactly 0 bytes, and the exit code is 0; adding extra arguments leaves both streams byte-identical under cmp. CAVEAT on the unqualified "no error / nothing on stderr": that clause fails at the kernel execve boundary, before the binary runs. A single extra argument of >= 131072 bytes (MAX_ARG_STRLEN) is rejected — bisected exactly: 131071 B -> rc=0 with 8 B stdout, 131072 B and 131073 B -> rc=126, 0 bytes stdout, and "Argument list too long" on stderr. This is a per-argument limit, not a total-size limit (control: two extras of 131071 B each, 262142 B total, succeed normally); the separate total-list limit ARG_MAX=2097152 trips between 2000 and 2100 extras of 1000 B. Since the process never starts in those cases, this is an environmental limit rather than a property of the binary's own argument handling, so it is not counted as a counterexample.
